paras: The Cherokee shooting of a man mistaken for Bob Hibble took place on the morning of August 27, 1910, near Cherokee, eighteen miles west of Tuscumbia, when a Black man hunted as Bob Hibble, a fugitive wanted for murder in Attalla County, Mississippi, was captured in a deserted schoolhouse and shot by officers before he surrendered. Officers who came from Attalla County two days later declared the prisoner to be the wrong man. Alabama papers followed the case for its leap from a fast train, the misidentification, and a Black woman's damage suit against the Southern Railway.

Bob Hibble was wanted in Attalla County, Mississippi, for the murder of Dewitt White, whom the first reports called "a white man" and later ones a deputy sheriff. A reward of $200 was offered for his capture. The date of White's killing varied from report to report: August 13 in one Florence dispatch, August 19 in a Tuscumbia dispatch, and "last month" in a second Florence dispatch.

According to a Tuscumbia dispatch to the Montgomery Advertiser, the conductor of a Southern passenger train wired ahead that he had aboard "a negro answering the description," and officers boarded at Cherokee. When they entered the coach with drawn revolvers and ordered the man to throw up his hands, he threw himself out of an open window while the train ran at fifty to sixty miles an hour. The train was stopped and backed to the spot, but no trace of him was found. The dispatches place the leap on different days, from the night of August 24 to August 26.

On the morning of August 27, John Sherrod and Al Horton found a man in a deserted schoolhouse on the W. P. Rutland place near Cherokee. The Birmingham Age-Herald's Florence correspondent wrote that he was "entirely nude" and that officers "had to shoot him before he surrendered." He was held in the Masonic hall at Cherokee to await officers from Mississippi, and a later report said he had been "filled with buckshot."

Officers who arrived from Attalla County on August 29 declared the prisoner at Cherokee "to be the wrong man," according to a Tuscumbia dispatch. The coverage does not give the wounded man's name, the extent of his wounds, or whether he was released.

In early September, Lassie Hamilton, described as "a negress," sued the Southern Railway for $3,000 in the Colbert County circuit court. She alleged that she fell and was hurt trying to get out of range when officers searching for Hibble drew guns on a Black passenger, and that an officer's profanity added to her injury. No report of the suit's outcome, or of any inquiry into the shooting, was found.

The case appears only in white Alabama dailies, mostly as brief special dispatches from Florence and Tuscumbia in the Birmingham Age-Herald, with one longer account in the Montgomery Advertiser; no Black-press coverage was found. Headlines centered on the fugitive and his escape, such as "Negro Escapes From Fast Moving Train" and "Leaps From Car Window," and the Age-Herald announced the capture as "Negro Murderer Again Captured," naming the prisoner a murderer before anyone had identified him. That report gave the officers' shooting as a necessity, saying they "had to shoot him."

The correction ran three days later under the heading "Wrong Negro Captured," noting that the man had risked his life and been shot "as the supposed Bob Hibble" but offering no comment on the shooting. The Age-Herald called Hamilton's suit "unique" and set out her allegations without comment.

The Florence dispatch of August 27 identified the captured man as Hibble, while the later Tuscumbia dispatch reported the Attalla officers' finding that he was not. One early dispatch placed Cherokee in Mississippi, but the other reports locate it eighteen miles west of Tuscumbia, and the related suit was heard in Colbert County.

reader.title: Cherokee shooting of a man mistaken for Bob Hibble
bases: Officers drew guns on a Black passenger and later shot a captured Black man before he surrendered, during an arrest on a Mississippi murder warrant; no mob or crowd is described (A2, A3, A4).
The train leap is reported by two papers (A1, A3), but the shooting at the capture appears only in the Birmingham Age-Herald, in two separate specials (A2, A4).

framing.detail: 'Negro Escapes From Fast Moving Train' and 'Leaps From Car Window' treat the leap as a daring escape by a 'desperate' fugitive.
'Negro Murderer Again Captured' names the prisoner a murderer and says officers 'had to shoot him'.
'Wrong Negro Captured' reports the misidentification without comment on the shooting.
'Railway Sued For Damages' calls the suit 'unique' and gives the plaintiff's allegations.
